## A Small Museum of Impossible Things

The museum stood between a bakery and a dentist’s office, behind a blue door that appeared only on rainy afternoons. Its brass sign read:

**MUSEUM OF IMPOSSIBLE THINGS**  
*Open whenever it rains.*

Inside, there were seven rooms.

The first contained a staircase that led upward but ended in a patch of blue sky. Children often climbed it, though adults usually saw only a locked door painted to resemble clouds. The second held a violin that played whatever its owner was feeling. The third contained an umbrella that remembered every raindrop it had ever sheltered.

In the fourth room, a glass jar was filled with the laughter of people who had not yet been born. Whenever the jar shook, someone far away suddenly laughed for no reason.

The fifth room was my favorite.

It held a small black-and-white photograph of my grandfather standing beside a train. He was young, smiling, holding a suitcase with one hand and a tiny paper moon with the other. I had never seen the picture before.

“You’re late,” said the curator.

She was an old woman in a green coat, though I suspected she was much younger than she looked. Perhaps she had simply been alive for a very long time.

“For the moon?” I asked.

“For the remembering.”

I looked at the photograph again. Behind the train, the sky was crowded with stars. The fields on either side glowed faintly, and in the distance, barely visible, stood my childhood house, its windows lit although it was broad daylight.

“My grandfather went missing in 1968,” I said. “The official story was that the train crashed.”

“Official stories are useful,” the curator replied. “They keep the weather out.”

She unlocked the glass case and removed the photograph. The paper moon cast a soft shadow across my palm.

“This was his last impossible thing,” she said. “He came to the museum carrying it. He wanted to return it to the person it belonged to, but he could no longer remember who that was.”

I turned the photograph over. On the back, in faded ink, were seven words:

**For the one who remembers tomorrow.**

The museum began to tremble gently. Somewhere, a clock chimed a number that did not exist. The jar of unborn laughter shook, and the violin in the next room played a melody I knew from childhood.

Then the front door opened, and cold rain swept into the hallway.

A man entered, shaking water from his coat. He was perhaps seventy years old. His hair was white, his face lined, and in his hand he carried a small paper moon.

It was exactly like the one in the photograph.

The curator smiled.

“Welcome back,” she said. “We’ve been waiting for you.”

The man looked at me. His eyes widened, and his face—older, tired, changed—held the same expression I had seen in the photograph.

“Hello, Grandfather,” I whispered.

He looked down at the moon in his hand.

“Hello,” he said, “future.”

Outside, the rain stopped. Through the narrow windows of the museum, I saw the street fill with evening, though it had been afternoon when I arrived. Stars appeared one by one, and somewhere beyond the bakery and the dentist’s office, a train began to whistle.

The curator placed the photograph between us.

“Most impossible things are lost because no one remembers where they came from,” she said. “But sometimes, if the right person comes back, they can continue.”

My grandfather held out the paper moon.

I took it.

It was warm as summer.

And when I looked toward the front door, I saw that the blue door had opened onto a platform under a sky crowded with stars. A train waited, its windows glowing gold.

The conductor rang the bell.

“Final stop,” he called. “All aboard.”

My grandfather offered me his hand.

I crossed the threshold with him, and the museum vanished behind us.

In the years that followed, I sometimes told the story of the place between the bakery and the dentist, the room that held a photograph of tomorrow, and the old man who had finally remembered where he was going.

No one ever believed me.

That was all right.

Impossible things require a little faith, and I had plenty left.
